parts.label: b

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q7:whole.hint: Separate the power emitted by the star from the power received per unit area at the observer.
notes: For isotropic emission, apparent brightness b = L/(4πd²). With parallax p in arcseconds, distance in parsecs is d = 1/p.
In a parallax diagram, p is the half-angle associated with a 1 AU baseline. For brightness ratios, distance enters as a square, so take a square root when solving for distance.

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q9:whole.hint: Check which way surface temperature increases on the horizontal axis before locating the star.
notes: On a standard H–R diagram luminosity increases upwards and temperature increases to the left. Red giants are luminous but cool; white dwarfs are hot but faint.
Use L = 4πR²σT⁴ to compare radii. A hotter star is not necessarily more luminous, because emitting area also matters.

sup-1cbc7e661452cc29-q1:whole.hint: Consider both the repulsion between nuclei and the chance of collisions while the fuel is confined.
notes: Fusion combines light nuclei into more tightly bound products. High temperature helps nuclei approach, high density increases collision rates, and confinement time allows reactions to occur.
Energy release comes from the mass difference or increase in total binding energy. High temperature is a condition for fusion; it is not the source of the released nuclear energy.

sup-1cbc7e661452cc29-q3:whole.hint: Identify the star’s initial mass and what fuel is being exhausted at the stage described.
notes: A star’s initial mass is the main determinant of its evolution. Low- and intermediate-mass stars can leave white dwarfs; sufficiently massive stars can undergo core-collapse supernovae and leave neutron stars or black holes.
Distinguish the ejected material, such as a planetary nebula, from the surviving remnant. Main-sequence stars are sustained mainly by hydrogen fusion in their cores.
